title: Variables: names, values and where they can be used
goal: Create a variable, rename it consistently, update its value and calculate a small total. Then explain a simple block boundary.

prerequisites.text: The types lesson introduced int price = 120; and distinguished type from value. We develop that skill here. No input, branching, loops or pointers are needed.

sections.title: Why give a number a name
paragraphs: Three notebooks at 120 currency units cost 360. You could write 120 * 3 directly in an output statement. But changing the price in multiple places makes it easy to miss one. A name such as price stores one current value and gives it meaning for a reader. The program does not understand the word “price”: humans supply the relationship to currency.

A variable connects a valid name, a type and a stored value. It is not an algebra equation that automatically recalculates other variables whenever something changes. Statements execute in order. If total received a product earlier, updating price does not update total without another assignment.

sections.title: Read int price = 120; part by part
paragraphs: int selects an integer type. price is the variable identifier, or name. = in this declaration introduces the initial value. 120 is an integer literal; ; ends the declaration. The variable is created with value 120. Read the whole line as “create the int variable price with initial value 120”.

For first identifiers, start with a Latin letter and continue with Latin letters, digits or _. Do not start with a digit, include spaces or use a keyword such as int. Case matters: price and Price are different identifiers. This is a convenient starting subset of C++ naming rules, not a claim that only Latin letters are allowed. Avoid leading underscores because some such names are reserved to the implementation.

tables.caption: Five parts of one line
rows: Introduces the initializer in a declaration

sections.title: Creating and updating are different actions
paragraphs: Later, price = 70; assigns a new value to the existing variable. Do not repeat int: we are not creating another price in the same block. First evaluate the right side, then store it in the variable on the left. Thus count = count - 1; reduces the previous count by one. It is not a mathematical assertion that count equals itself minus one.

In the example, count remains 3. Before the price update, 120 * 3 gives 360; after price = 70, 70 * 3 gives 210. The program state has changed. Before continuing, identify which value changed and which stayed the same.

sections.title: Rename consistently
paragraphs: Rename price to unitPrice in your own copy. Change the declaration and every use of that variable: both products and the assignment. Output should stay 360 and 210. We changed a name, not the data or calculation rule.

If you change only the declaration, the compiler will encounter the old unknown name price. Do not add another variable just to silence the error; find the inconsistent use. Replacing * with + compiles but gives 73 rather than 210 for 70 and 3. A naming error is found by compilation; the wrong operation is found by comparison with the task.

sections.title: Where a name is available
paragraphs: Braces can enclose a separate block inside main. A local name declared in that block can be used after its declaration within its scope; it does not become available outside. In this example, delivery is read inside the extra braces and price in the surrounding main body. This is a first simple scope case; lifetime, pointers and complex shadowing are unnecessary here.

Moving the delivery output after the inner block makes that name unavailable there. The computation did not randomly forget a digit: the source uses a name outside its scope. Fix the location of the use, or deliberately declare the necessary variable in the surrounding block. Do not delete braces at random.

sections.title: Now make a different calculation
paragraphs: Four kits were booked for class at 25 currency units each. One kit was cancelled. In the task, update count using count = count - 1; before calculating total. Expect three remaining kits and a total of 75. There is no hidden requirement to write a cancellation condition: the one cancellation is given.

After checking, explain the order of statements. If total is computed before reducing count, it stays 100 until explicitly recalculated. Correct output together with that explanation shows more than a matching number: you traced a state change. This finishes the starting route; you can then return to the full 67-topic programme.

practice.title: On your own: one cancellation
practice.task: Initially there are 4 kits at 25 each. One is cancelled. In your starter, reduce count by one before calculating total, then produce remaining=3 and total=75. Rename price consistently to unitPrice. No input or if is needed.
practice.stdinNote: Leave the input field empty: this task sets every value in the program.
criteria: total is calculated after the count update and equals 75.
Renaming is consistent; initialization and assignment are explained.
practice.hint: count - 1 uses the previous count. Store that result before calculating total.

passport.goal: Update a value and calculate a new result.
passport.start: price=25, count=4; the starter calculates before cancellation.
passport.knowledge: Declaration, assignment, multiplication, output and identifiers.
passport.change: Add one assignment and rename every use of price.
passport.inputs: Values are already in the program; stdin is empty.
passport.checks: Run and compare both lines; explain statement order separately.
passport.errors: Total computed before cancellation; inconsistent rename.
passport.recovery: Undo the last edit; return to your own saved state without loading the reference into the editor.

exercises.task: In your copy of the example, rename price to unitPrice and retain output 360/210.
exercises.criteria: The name changes everywhere, while values and output remain the same.

selfcheck.prompt: What does = do in int price = 120;?
options: Introduces the initial value when creating the variable
selfcheck.feedback: This is a declaration with initialization. The later price = 70; is assignment.

selfcheck.prompt: count=4; total=25*count; count=count-1; What value is already stored in total?
selfcheck.feedback: total does not automatically recalculate after count changes.

selfcheck.prompt: Where can delivery, declared in an inner block, be used?
options: Within its scope after the declaration
selfcheck.feedback: The surrounding code does not gain that local name.

selfcheck.prompt: After renaming price to unitPrice, what must change?
options: The declaration and every use of that variable
selfcheck.feedback: The name must be consistent; the values can stay the same.

selfcheck.prompt: Read int price = 120;, distinguish initialization from assignment and explain the calculation order after cancelling one kit.
selfcheck.feedback: Compare your explanation with the walkthrough; it is not graded automatically.
